title: The Main Story: DHS Bought an Air Force and Forgot the Pilots
dek: Ten planes, $464 million, no competition, because the deportations could not wait. Eleven months later: two flights, a Gulfstream for the FBI director, a 737 with a bar nobody will take, a $41 million markup on one March morning, and a FOIA letter that cited a criminal investigation before the department took it back.
body:
Let's start with the good news, because there is some. On Wednesday and Thursday of this week, two Boeing 737s owned by the Department of Homeland Security flew from Texas to Mexico carrying people being deported [10][11]. That is a sentence the department has been promising to make true since last November, when it spent $464 million, without competition, on ten airplanes it said were so urgently needed for deportation flights that it did not have time to ask anyone else for a price [1][5]. Eleven months later: two flights. If you bought a car in November, insisted the dealer skip the paperwork because you were in such a hurry, and then drove it for the first time on Halloween, your family would be holding a meeting about you [1][11].

Tonight: the ten planes, the one morning, the one donor, the one FOIA letter that said the quiet part out loud, and the one word Kristi Noem is prepared to go to the mat over [1][2][8].

## An air force with no air crew

Here is the fleet, as The New York Times found it in August. Seven used Boeing 737 passenger jets, parked at Chennault International Airport in Lake Charles, Louisiana, for months at a time [1]. Why parked? An internal government document explained it with the plainness of a Post-it on a broken coffee machine: the department did not have the staff to fly them [1]. It had bought seven airliners and forgotten the pilots, which is the kind of mistake you can make with a model kit, not with a line item [1].

Then the department tried to fix it the way you'd expect. It put out a solicitation for a contractor to supply crews and mechanics, starting in the summer of 2027 [1]. The summer of 2027! The urgency was so unusual and so compelling that the plan to address it is a year and a half out, which is not urgency, that is a kitchen renovation [1][5].

Meanwhile, how many flights had ICE managed to charter from private companies, the old-fashioned, boring, working way, during the same administration? About 25,800, according to Human Rights First's flight tracker [1]. ICE's former acting director under President Obama, John Sandweg, told the Times that owning planes would not have made the agency's top ten needs [1]. It is not clear it would have made the top forty. The top ten needs of an agency that chartered 25,800 flights are pretty well covered by the chartering [1].

## The three planes that did fly, and whom they flew

Now, three of the ten aircraft were not passenger 737s. They were business jets, and business jets, unlike deportation planes, found work immediately [1]. One Gulfstream G650 went to the FBI on a twelve-month lease to carry Director Kash Patel, at a rate the Times reported was less than the bureau would pay a private operator [1]. So the deportation fleet's first confirmed mission was a discount lease to the FBI director, which is a bit like learning the fire truck you bought is being used as a limo, but at least it's a cheap limo [1][4].

The second G650 is being refitted for the border czar, Tom Homan, and other senior officials, according to the Senate appropriators who read the department's own description of the plan [4]. And the third jet is the showpiece: a Boeing 737 MAX 8 converted into a private aircraft with a bedroom, a shower, a kitchen and a bar, since repainted in the color scheme of the new Air Force One [1][4]. The department told senators it is removing the bedroom [4]. It tried to lend the whole plane to the Pentagon, which said no agreement was ever signed, which is the diplomatic way of saying the Pentagon has its own planes and also its own bar [1].

As for the seven that were supposed to deport people: by August the department had told the Senate that four of them would instead fly members of Congress on overseas trips, leaving three for the stated purpose [1][4]. Three out of ten. The department bought a deportation fleet in which the deportation share is thirty percent, and the rest is a travel agency for the people who are supposed to be investigating it [4].

## The morning of March 24

The second Times story, in October, is about one morning. Markwayne Mullin was sworn in to replace Noem on the afternoon of March 24. That morning, with hours left in her tenure, the department agreed to buy the last five planes from Daedalus Aviation Corporation of Arlington, Virginia, a company that until 2025 had never held a federal contract [1][2][3].

The prices, per the Times: $108 million for the converted 737 MAX 8, which Daedalus had bought a few months earlier for less than $90 million; $106 million for the two Gulfstreams, which had cost Daedalus about $83 million; and $45 million each for two older passenger 737s, which six aviation market specialists said was far above what such planes sell for [2][3]. Add the markups the paper could document and you get more than $41 million, in one morning, for being the only bidder in a hurry [2].

Mullin, the Times reported, considered backing out, then worried the department would lose even more money by doing so, and the White House chief of staff, Susie Wiles, advised him to let it go through [3]. Which means the incoming secretary looked at the purchase, recognized it as a bad idea, and signed anyway because the previous secretary had set it up so that walking away cost more than staying, the classic exit strategy of the timeshare and now, apparently, of the Cabinet [3].

The department's position is that the deal was made and approved before Mullin was sworn in [1][3]. Noem's spokesperson says it was finalized under Mullin [1]. They are both pointing at March 24, from opposite ends of the day, and the $303 million landed in the middle [1][5].

## The word she wants retracted

Noem, now a special envoy at the State Department, posted a letter to the Times on the day the October story ran, demanding a retraction or a correction, and her central objection is not to the $41 million, or the parked planes, or the bedroom [2][3]. It is to the word “donor” [2].

The facts in dispute: William Walters, Daedalus's chairman and a former State Department surgeon, gave $10,000 in October 2024 to American Resolve, a political committee the Times says was created to advance Noem's political interests, and whose sister nonprofit paid her adviser Corey Lewandowski $265,500 in consulting fees [2][3][6]. Daedalus says Walters did not know the committee was tied to Noem when he wrote the check [1][2]. That is the defense: our chairman gave ten thousand dollars to a committee with Noem's picture on its website, and it was a complete coincidence that it was Noem's [3]. The Times said it stands by the story [2].

In fairness to Noem, the donor is not even the biggest Walters story. The same POGO investigation that found the committee's Lewandowski payments also found that Walters's companies, in one office building in Arlington, hold the up-to-$915 million contract to run the self-deportation program and leased the department its first private 737, the one staff nicknamed the Big, Beautiful Jet, which flew Noem to Amman in December and, according to Axios, the first lady between Washington and New York in March [6][7]. Noem told lawmakers she had been on it once [6]. Once is also how many times, per Congress's count, the plan to buy any of these planes was authorized, which is to say Senate appropriators say it was not [4].

## The FOIA letter that answered a different question

Then there is the letter nobody at the department meant to send. On October 14, a reporter at The Washington Sun filed a Freedom of Information Act request for the acquisition memo on seven 737s and a Gulfstream, plus the bills of sale and the policy on which officials get to ride [8]. The department's privacy office wrote back that it could neither confirm nor deny the records existed, because the purchases were tied to an “ongoing criminal law enforcement investigation” [8].

Now, there are two ways to read that. One is that the department has an actual criminal investigation into its own airplane purchases and accidentally told a newspaper. The other is that a FOIA officer reached for the wrong template. Six days later, after the Sun published the letter, the department chose option two and said the response had been sent in error [8]. The Justice Department said it does not confirm or deny investigations, the FBI and the White House referred the question back to the department, and the records, some of which are named in the department's own contracting filings, remain where they were, which is nowhere you can read them [8].

Two days after that, The Wall Street Journal reported that the Justice Department is reviewing allegations that Lewandowski profited from his unpaid role as Noem's top adviser, after a criminal referral from the department's inspector general, whose investigators found evidence he may have been involved in improperly awarding contracts [9]. Lewandowski's lawyer says he has not been contacted and denies wrongdoing [9]. Asked about it, President Trump said he wants his people to be honest, and that if they are not, they have to be prosecuted, which is a sentence that sounds better the fewer times you have had to say it [9].

## What the Senate got for its letters

Congress, to its credit, noticed, and did the thing Congress does. On August 12, Senators Patty Murray and Chris Murphy wrote to Mullin, counted twelve aircraft bought with last year's reconciliation money including five luxury jets, said the department had no legal authority to buy any of them, and asked it to sell the planes, give the money back, and hand over the contracts, flight logs and the FBI lease by August 26 [4]. On August 25, Senators Blumenthal, Welch and Schiff sent ten questions, starting with the one that still has no public answer: how did the department find Daedalus in the first place, and who made the call [5]?

As of October 7, neither letter had received a reply [2]. The letters asked for documents. The department has instead spent the fall explaining which day a purchase happened, which word a newspaper used, and which template a FOIA officer grabbed [1][2][8].

Here is what we know for certain. The department said it needed ten planes so urgently that it could not wait for a second offer [1][5]. It then waited eleven months to fly two of them, gave one to the FBI, offered one to the Pentagon, assigned four to congressional travel, and solicited pilots for 2027 [1][4][10]. The only thing about this program that moved fast was the morning of March 24 [2][3]. That's the main story. The receipts are below.

pt.title: A matéria principal: o DHS comprou uma força aérea e esqueceu os pilotos
pt.dek: Dez aviões, US$ 464 milhões, sem concorrência, porque as deportações não podiam esperar. Onze meses depois: dois voos, um Gulfstream para o diretor do FBI, um 737 com bar que ninguém quer, um ágio de US$ 41 milhões numa manhã de março e uma resposta a pedido de informação que citou uma investigação criminal antes de o departamento recuar.

de.title: Die Hauptgeschichte: Das DHS kaufte eine Luftwaffe und vergaß die Piloten
de.dek: Zehn Flugzeuge, 464 Millionen Dollar, keine Ausschreibung, weil die Abschiebungen nicht warten konnten. Elf Monate später: zwei Flüge, ein Gulfstream für den FBI-Direktor, eine 737 mit Bar, die niemand will, 41 Millionen Dollar Aufschlag an einem Märzmorgen und ein Auskunftsbescheid, der eine strafrechtliche Ermittlung nannte, ehe das Ministerium ihn zurücknahm.
